title: Trees, tries, and union-find: choosing a structure for relationships
sources: Python standard library: dict, set, list, and recursion concepts
Python documentation: data-model and collection-operation concepts
masterChecklist: Searching, sorting, hashing, heaps, trees, graphs, shortest paths, traversals, union-find, tries
Core data structures: arrays/lists, stacks, queues, dequeues, hash tables, linked structures, priority queues, trees, graphs
Problem decomposition, specifications, preconditions/postconditions, invariants, and proofs by reasoning
whyItMatters: Many real problems are about relationships: a category hierarchy, autocomplete prefixes, or groups that become connected as events arrive. Choosing the matching structure makes the rule shorter and avoids repeatedly scanning everything.
simpleExplanation: A tree represents parent-to-child relationships. A trie stores text by shared prefixes, which can make prefix lookup natural. Union-find (also called disjoint-set) tracks which items belong to the same connected group while new connections are added.
mentalModel: A tree is an organization chart. A trie is a library of words sharing the same first shelves. Union-find is a set of name badges that merge into one table whenever two people are introduced.
outcomes: Recognize when a hierarchy, prefix lookup, or evolving connectivity problem is present.
Represent a simple tree/trie with nested dictionaries safely.
Use find and union operations to track groups.
State the invariant that each union-find root represents a group.
Avoid choosing a complex structure when a plain list or dictionary is simpler.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learning platform suggests lessons as a learner types and groups learners who are connected through a study-team graph.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: The platform scans every possible word for every keystroke and repeatedly traverses all relationships to see whether two learners are already connected.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Use a prefix-oriented index for suggestions where the vocabulary/ranking need justifies it, and union-find when connections arrive incrementally and only group membership is needed.

explanation: Initially every item is its own parent, so every item is a one-member group.
find follows parent links until it reaches a root: an item whose parent is itself.
union joins two roots only when they differ; joining an already-connected pair changes nothing.
The assignment inside find shortens a path for future lookups. This is called path compression.
This compact example omits validation and union-by-rank/size; production code should define behavior for unknown items and scale requirements.
workedExample.expectedOutput: True because ana and ben were joined, then False because cam remains separate.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Add union('ben', 'cam') and observe that all three now share a root. Then call union again to see the no-op behavior.

procedure: Describe the query first: hierarchy traversal, prefix lookup, or same-group membership.
Choose a simple representation and state its invariant before optimizing.
For a tree, ensure child relationships cannot accidentally form a cycle if your domain requires a hierarchy.
For a trie, decide normalization, case handling, memory limits, and whether prefix results need ranking.
For union-find, initialize each known item as its own root and validate unknown input.
Test small examples: separate groups, a merge, repeated merge, and a lookup after several merges.
Measure before introducing specialized structures; a dictionary or sorted list can be clearer for a small dataset.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using union-find when the application needs the actual shortest route between two items.
commonMistakes.why: Union-find answers whether items are connected, not which path connects them.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use graph traversal/pathfinding when route information matters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a general graph as a tree without checking for cycles or multiple parents.
commonMistakes.why: Tree traversal assumptions can fail or loop on arbitrary relationships.
commonMistakes.avoid: Define the data invariant and track visited nodes for graph traversal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building a trie for a tiny fixed word list without measuring need.
commonMistakes.why: It adds code and memory overhead where a simple filter may be clearer.
commonMistakes.avoid: Choose the simplest structure that meets the observed requirement.

lab.title: Group study teams with a tiny union-find
lab.safety: Uses local dictionaries only. It does not query people, networks, or external systems.
guidedSteps: A root is an item where parent[item] == item.
Make find return the root for a known item.
Call find for both union inputs.
Point one root at the other only if they differ.
Assert group membership before and after a second merge.
checks: Returns a root for each known item.
Does not change already-joined groups unnecessarily.
States that this does not provide a route/path.
lab.solutionExplanation: The parent map is a compact representation of groups. find discovers a group's representative; union merges representatives. The final assertion shows transitive connectivity after cam is joined through ben.
challenges: Predict the result of union('ana', 'ben') after they are already joined.
Find the bug: pointing an arbitrary member instead of a root without checking its group.
Experiment: add a fourth learner and form two separate teams before merging them.
lab.testCode:
assert find('ana')==find('ben')==find('cam')
assert find('ana')=='ana'
print('PASS: union-find roots')

projectConnection.milestone: Use a tree or graph representation for lesson relationships, then add a local union-find simulation that answers whether two study members belong to the same merged team.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: The project distinguishes hierarchy, route, prefix, and connectivity questions; it selects the matching structure and tests its stated invariant.

assessment.question: What question is union-find designed to answer well?
assessment.answer: Whether two items are in the same connected group as connections are added.
assessment.explanation: It does not supply the path between them.

assessment.question: What does a trie organize by?
assessment.answer: Shared prefixes of sequences such as words.
assessment.explanation: That makes prefix-oriented lookup natural when the extra structure is justified.

assessment.question: What invariant does a union-find root have?
assessment.answer: A root is its own parent and represents one connected group.
assessment.explanation: find follows parent links until it reaches that representative.
